title: Almost stochastic dominance via optimal transport

p.t: The fundamental aim of classical stochastic dominance theory is to provide order relations between probability measures for comparing random quantities; see e.g. Müller and Stoyan (2002) and Shaked and Shanthikumar (2007) and the references therein for an overview. The most famous example of such an order relation is what is often called the stochastic order in probability theory or also first-order stochastic dominance in more applied literature. We will write X ≤ st Y for random elements in an arbitrary partially ordered Polish space, if one of the following two equivalent conditions holds: (i) E[u(X)] ≤ E[u(Y )] for all increasing functions for which the expectations exist, (ii) there exists a coupling X d = X and Ỹ d = Y with X ≤ Ỹ P -a.s. These equivalent formulations explain why stochastic dominance is useful in decision theory, probability, and optimization: if X ≤ st Y , then every rational decision maker who prefers more to less will prefer Y to X . This economic interpretation can be found for the univariate case already in Hadar and Russell (1969). The general result of the equivalence for arbitrary partially ordered Polish spaces is based on a theorem in Strassen (1965) and can be found e.g. in Kamae et al. (1977). A drawback of this formulation is that exact stochastic dominance is often too demanding. Suppose, for instance, that a random payoff is compared with a fixed benchmark. If the random payoff can fall below the benchmark with positive probability, then first-order stochastic dominance of the random payoff over the benchmark is impossible. As another example, consider multivariate normal distributions X ∼ N (µ, Σ) , Y ∼ N (µ ′ , Σ ′ ) with values in R d . Then X ≤ st Y only holds if µ ≤ µ ′ and Σ = Σ ′ , see Müller (2001).

Clearly the requirement of having the exactly same covariance matrices is very restrictive. Parametric families of concepts of almost stochastic dominance with a parameter γ ∈ [0, 1] have been introduced to relax these restrictive requirements, where γ = 0 corresponds to ≤ st and larger parameters lead to weaker orderings. One route is to restrict the class of utility functions, excluding marginal utilities that are too extreme. In the univariate theory of Leshno and Levy (2002) and Müller et al. (2017), the relevant classes control the ratio between small and large marginal utilities. These approaches have an important structural feature: for each fixed parameter they define genuine transitive order relations, not merely numerical indices of deviation from dominance. On the real line, the same idea can be described geometrically. For integrable real-valued random variables X and Y , let F and G be their distribution functions. The failure of X ≤ st Y is measured by one of the two one-sided areas between F and G , while the compensating part is measured by the other. Using quantiles, these quantities are where we have used the notation x + := max(x, 0) . The condition for univariate γalmost stochastic dominance can then be written as D + (X, Y ) ≤ γD -(X, Y ) . In the special case where a random payoff is compared with a sure benchmark, this is a gain-loss comparison closely related to the Omega ratio of Keating and Shadwick (2002).

Optimal transport gives a natural language for these one-sided quantities. For the asym- where the infimum is taken over all couplings of X and Ỹ . The second equality holds as the monotone quantile coupling is optimal for convex costs on the real line; see Cambanis et al. (1976), and Villani (2009) for a general introduction to optimal transport. More generally, if E is partially ordered and c(x, y) = 0 precisely when x ≤ y , then, under the usual closedness and integrability assumptions, the coupling characterization of X ≤ st Y can be stated in equivalent terms as OT c (X, Y ) = 0 . This observation goes back at least to Hansel and Troallic (1978), who have shown the relation of the theorem in Strassen (1965) to the Ford-Fulkerson theorem. This observation was also the starting point for the definition of the OT-based versions of multivariate almost stochastic dominance recently introduced by Rioux et al. (2024). These contributions show that optimal transport is a flexible way to measure deviations from stochastic dominance and to construct tests or diagnostics for such deviations. However, measuring a deviation from stochastic dominance is not the same as defining an order relation. If one declares X to be dominated by Y whenever a transport ratio is below a fixed threshold, the resulting threshold relation need not be transitive. This problem already appears in one dimension for ratios based on squared Wasserstein-type costs, as in the transport versions of del Barrio et al. (2018) and Rioux et al. (2024); see Example A.1 in the Appendix. The same mechanism applies to more general costs generated by convex functions h through c(x, y) = h(x -y) . Thus such ratios can be useful measures of distance from stochastic dominance, but they do not by themselves provide partial orders suitable for decision making, see e.g. Álvarez-Esteban et al. (2017) for a detailed discussion of this problem of non-transitivity of decisions based on such tests for stochastic dominance. The exceptional case is the linear absolute-value cost h(x) = |x| , where the threshold relation reduces to the classical univariate almost stochastic dominance order of Leshno and Levy (2002).

This paper starts from the above distinction. Our goal is not only to quantify how far a pair of laws is from stochastic dominance, but to define an almost dominance relation that remains a partial order, where we can compute the best possible parameter by solving an optimal transportation problem. The modification is simple in the univariate case. Since The denominator is not a symmetric transport distance. It is the violation cost plus the compensating increase in a benchmark functional, here the mean. This reformulation has the advantage that we only have to solve one optimal transport problem instead of two. This is the feature that survives in the general construction outlined in the main part of the paper and is responsible for transitivity. We will generalize this idea to the multivariate setting, and even to general partially ordered Polish spaces. The test function characterization of the univariate concept introduced in Leshno and Levy (2002) can naturally be generalized to the multivariate setting. This has been done in Müller et al. (2025). They consider as the most natural extension for γ ∈ [0, 1] the class U γ of continuously differentiable utilities u : R d → R satisfying γ ≤ ∂u ∂x i (x) ≤ 1 for all x ∈ R d and i = 1, . . . , d. Their version of almost stochastic dominance with a parameter γ ∈ [0, 1] then holds between random vectors X and Y , if E[u(X)] ≤ E[u(Y)] for all u ∈ U γ . Müller et al. (2025) derive sufficient conditions for γ , but these are far from the best possible γ in concrete examples.

One of the main aims of this paper is to show that the best possible γ for this version of almost stochastic dominance can be derived by solving an appropriate optimal transportation problem and defining an equivalent ordering based on the solution of the OT problem.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 recalls quasi-pseudometrics, their induced orders, and the coupling characterization of first-order stochastic dominance. Section 3 introduces the best possible coefficient γ * , proves the partial order, duality, and robustness results, and then specializes them to R d . Section 4 contains two numerical illustrations: day-by-day sunshine measurements for Rome and Siegen as considered in an example by Müller et al. (2025), and the bivariate Gaussian example of Range and Østerdal (2019). Section 5 contains the proofs of the main results. The Appendix collects the non-transitivity example for the Wasserstein-ratio criterion and a Banach-lattice example of quasi-pseudo-metrics that explains why we typically choose p = 1 for the L p -type distances used in our examples.

Definition 2.1. The mapping d is called a pseudo-metric, if it satisfies in addition the property (iii) d(x, y) = d(y, x) for all x, y ∈ E , and the pseudo-metric is a metric, if in addition (iv) d(x, y) = 0 if and only if x = y . We next recall the notion of an order on E . Definition 2.2. For a relation R ⪯ ⊆ E × E we also write x ⪯ y , if (x, y) ∈ R ⪯ . The relation ⪯ is called a preorder if it has the following two properties: (i) x ⪯ x for all x ∈ E , (ii) x ⪯ y and y ⪯ z implies x ⪯ z for all x, y, z ∈ E . The relation ⪯ is called a (partial) order relation, if it fulfills in addition the property that (iii) x ⪯ y and y ⪯ x implies x = y . Given a quasi-pseudo-metric d one can define a preorder ≤ d via , which is a pseudometric and indeed a metric, if the corresponding preorder ≤ d + is an order relation. The simplest example for this is the case of the classical Euclidean distance of the real numbers with d + (x, y) = (x -y) + so that the corresponding partial order is the classical ordering of real numbers:
x ≤ d + y if and only if x ≤ y. A natural extension of this is given by a general Banach lattice as described e.g. in the book of Schaefer (1974), see Example A.2.

p.t: We let X R and X S be random vectors with empirical laws Law(X R ) := 1 N N i=1 δ x i R and Law(X S ) := 1 N N i=1 δ x i S and aim to compute the coefficient for the cost function c(x, y) = d i=1 (x i -y i ) + and g(x) = d i=1 x i . In this way we determine the threshold γ * such that X S ≤ γ X R holds for any γ ≥ γ * according to Theorem 3.8. Algorithm 1: Auction algorithm: X are the "bidders" and Y are the "objects", b(x, y) represents the benefit of the assignment σ(x) = y . To find OT c (X S , X R ) we run the Auction Algorithm 1 (Bertsekas, 1990) with b ≡ -c This type of algorithm uses OT duality and is based on the idea of an auction. The aim is to approximate the Kantorovich potential and its c -conjugate via a bidding procedure: start with some candidate function f : Y → R and think of f (y) as the price of y ∈ Y . If x wants to buy y (because its price is low), then y is assigned to x and the price f (y) of y is increased just to the point that y is as desirable for x as the second best object. One then picks the next unassigned bidder x , assigns another object to x and raises its price via the same principle. This leads to the following observation: as the prices f can only increase over time, any object y assigned to x will stay the best choice for x until it is assigned to another bidder. The bidding is iterated until all the objects Y are assigned to the owners X ; the optimality of the resulting assignment is then implied by the observation we just made. Importantly for application, the complexity of the Auction algorithm scales linearly in d . This is the principal reason why we use it here, and why we consider it particularly well suited to high-dimensional applications.

p.s: Comparison of sunshine in Rome and Siegen
p.t: We compute γ * for each year separately. The results are shown in Figure 2. According to the data, the coefficient γ * is quite stable over the years, with values ranging from 0.11 to 0.16.
